samples.text:
Governments and companies spend a lot of money on scientific research every year. Some people think this money should only go to research which has practical benefit, not research that only increase our knowledge. I disagree with this opinion.

Firstly, it is very difficult to know which research will be useful in the future. Many important inventions came from research that seemed to have no practical use at the beginning. For example, scientists studied electricity and light many years ago only because they were curious, but now we use this knowledge for computers, phones and medicine. If they only did research with clear benefit, we might not have this technology today.

Secondly, knowledge itself has value. Humans always want to understand the world, for example how the universe began or how the brain is working. This kind of research makes our life more rich and it inspires young people to study science. Also, pure research gives the base for practical research. Engineers and doctors use the discoveries of basic science to create new products and treatments.

However, I understand that the money for research is limited. When there are serious problems like diseases or climate change, it makes sense to give more money to research which can solve them quickly. People who pay taxes wants to see results from the money they give.

In conclusion, I disagree that scientific research should be funded only for practical benefits. Both kinds of research are important, and governments should give money to research that increase human knowledge as well, because in the future it can bring many benefits that we cannot imagine now.

samples.text:
With limited public budgets, many people argue that scientific research should be funded according to its likely practical benefits rather than simply to expand human knowledge. While I accept that applied research deserves significant support, I disagree with making practical value the main criterion for funding decisions.

It is understandable why some prefer to focus on practical outcomes. Research is expensive, and governments must justify their spending to taxpayers who expect visible results, such as new medical treatments, cleaner energy or improved crops. When societies face urgent challenges like pandemics or climate change, directing money towards solving them seems both logical and responsible.

However, the history of science shows that the most transformative discoveries often come from research with no obvious application at the time. Scientists who investigated the structure of atoms or the behaviour of light were motivated largely by curiosity, yet their work eventually led to technologies ranging from medical imaging to the internet. Had funding been limited to projects with predictable benefits, many of these breakthroughs might never have happened. The problem is that practical value is extremely difficult to predict in advance.

Furthermore, basic research provides the foundation that applied science depends on. Engineers and medical researchers build on theories and data produced by scientists who were simply trying to understand how the natural world works. Reducing support for fundamental research would therefore weaken applied research in the long term, since there would be fewer new ideas to develop.

In my view, a balanced system is needed, in which a substantial part of funding goes to curiosity-driven research selected for its scientific quality, while specific programmes target pressing practical problems.

In conclusion, although practical benefits are important, I do not think they should determine all research funding. Supporting the expansion of knowledge for it's own sake is essential, as it is frequently the source of the most valuable practical advances.

samples.text:
Decisions about which scientific research to fund have become increasingly contested, with some arguing that public money should be directed primarily towards projects likely to yield practical benefits. I disagree with this position. Although applied research clearly merits substantial investment, making practical utility the principal test for funding would, paradoxically, reduce the practical returns of science over time.

The case for prioritising applied research is not without force. Governments are accountable to taxpayers, and when resources are scarce it seems reasonable to favour work that promises better treatments, more efficient energy or safer infrastructure. In the face of pressing problems such as antibiotic resistance, research with clear objectives offers a tangible sense of progress.

The central difficulty, however, is that the usefulness of knowledge can rarely be foreseen. Many of the technologies that define modern life emerged from inquiries pursued for their own sake: studies of quantum behaviour made possible the semiconductors in every smartphone, while research into obscure bacteria provided the tools behind modern gene editing. No funding committee assessing these projects at the outset could have predicted such outcomes. A system that rewards only anticipated benefits would systematically overlook the unexpected discoveries that often prove most valuable.

Fundamental research also sustains the wider scientific ecosystem. It trains highly skilled researchers, generates the theoretical frameworks on which applied work depends and keeps a country at the frontier of knowledge. Moreover, there is intrinsic worth in understanding the origins of the universe or the workings of the mind, questions that reflect a basic human aspiration and inspire future generations of scientists.

The most sensible approach is therefore a portfolio: dedicated funding for mission-driven research on urgent problems, alongside secure support for curiosity-driven work judged on its scientific merit.

In conclusion, while practical benefits matter, they should not be the dominant criterion for funding science, since the pursuit of knowledge itself remains the most reliable source of future innovation.
